citations.quote: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. If Omega has the specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, then $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F=\sum_j\int_{S_j}F\cdot\nu_j\,dS$, with faces counted once off E. All integrals are finite. In a specified finite gluing, the two fluxes on every shared face cancel.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

derivations.claim: (The cone condition (a).) By [L1], $\lambda:=b/a+1$ gives $z^{\mathsf T}(\lambda A^0+\xi_iA^i)z\ge((b/a+1)a-b)|z|^2=|z|^2>0$ for $z\ne0$ and $|\xi|\le1$; so the quadratic form is positive definite, in particular nonnegative. This is (a).

(The cone inequality.) Suppose $w$ solves the system and put $j^\mu:=w^{\mathsf T}A^\mu w$, a $C^1$ vector field. Then $\operatorname{div}_{(t,x)}j=\partial_t(w^{\mathsf T}A^0w)+\partial_i(w^{\mathsf T}A^iw)=2w^{\mathsf T}(A^0\partial_tw+A^i\partial_iw)+w^{\mathsf T}(\partial_tA^0+\partial_iA^i)w=-2w^{\mathsf T}Cw+w^{\mathsf T}(\partial_tA^0+\partial_iA^i)w\le K'w^{\mathsf T}w\le(K'/a)j^0$, where $K':=2K+\sup|\partial_tA^0+\partial_iA^i|$.

(Flux through the truncated cone.) For $0<\tau<t_0$ let $D_\tau:=\{(s,x):0\le s\le\tau,\ |x-x_0|\le\lambda(t_0-s)\}$, so that $\partial D_\tau$ consists of the base $B_0:=\{(0,x):|x-x_0|\le\lambda t_0\}$, the lateral surface $L_\tau:=\{ |x-x_0|=\lambda(t_0-s),\ 0\le s\le\tau\}$, and the top $B_\tau:=\{\tau\}\times\{|x-x_0|\le\lambda(t_0-\tau)\}$. On the base the outward normal is $-\partial_t$, so the flux is $-\int_{B_0}j^0$; on the top it is $+\int_{B_\tau}j^0$; on the lateral surface the outward unit normal is $\nu=(\lambda,\xi)/\sqrt{1+\lambda^2}$ with $\xi=(x-x_0)/|x-x_0|$ and $|\xi|=1$, so the flux is $(1+\lambda^2)^{-1/2}\int_{L_\tau}w^{\mathsf T}(\lambda A^0+\xi_iA^i)w\,dS\ge0$ by (a). Integrating the inequality of step 1.2 over $D_\tau$ and using the divergence theorem [L2] gives $E(\tau):=\int_{B_\tau}j^0\le\int_{B_0}j^0+(K'/a)\int_0^\tau E(s)\,ds-\int_{L_\tau}(\cdots)\le\int_{B_0}j^0+(K'/a)\int_0^\tau E(s)\,ds$, since the lateral flux is nonnegative.

(Conclusion (b).) If the data vanish on $B_0$, then $E(\tau)\le(K'/a)\int_0^\tau E(s)\,ds$; since $E\ge0$ is continuous (even absolutely continuous) in $\tau$, Gronwall [L3] gives $E=0$ on $[0,t_0)$, hence $w=0$ on $\bigcup_{\tau<t_0}\overline{D_\tau}=D$ by continuity. This is (b).

(Independence (c).) If two systems agree on a neighborhood of $D$ and their solutions agree on $B_0$, then $w:=w_1-w_2$ solves a linear system of the same form with the common leading coefficients $A^\mu$ and with $C$ the coefficient of the difference (a bounded smooth matrix built from the two zeroth-order coefficients, using that the equations coincide on the neighborhood), and $w=0$ on $B_0$; step 3.1 applies and gives $w=0$ on $D$. This is (c).

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

If $R$ is a commutative ring, $n\geq1$, $A\in M_n(R)$, and $\det(A)$ is a
unit, then

$$A^{-1}=\det(A)^{-1}\operatorname{adj}(A).$$

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\geq 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$, with rows and columns indexed by
$0,\ldots,n-1$ ([[def-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]]).

For $0\leq i,j<n$, the **deleted-row-and-column matrix** $A^{(i,j)}$ is
obtained by deleting row $i$ and column $j$. The **minor** and **cofactor** at
$(i,j)$ are

$$M_{ij}(A):=\det(A^{(i,j)}),\qquad C_{ij}(A):=\varepsilon_{ij}M_{ij}(A),$$

where the sign is taken in $R$ by parity: $\varepsilon_{ij}:=1_R$ when $i+j$ is
even and $\varepsilon_{ij}:=-1_R$ when $i+j$ is odd. Writing this as
$(-1)^{i+j}$ is the usual abbreviation; it is the ring element $-1_R$ raised to
a natural-number power in $R$, not a real power. When $n=1$,
$A^{(0,0)}$ is the unique $0\times0$ matrix and its determinant is defined
locally to be $1$. For $n>1$, the determinant is the published matrix
determinant ([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]).

The **cofactor matrix** is
$\operatorname{cof}(A):=(C_{ij}(A))$, and the **adjugate** is

$$\operatorname{adj}(A):=\operatorname{cof}(A)^{\mathsf T},$$

using the published transpose operation
([[def-ring-matrix-product-identity-and-transpose]]).

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is
$$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$
The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), let $f : X \to Y$ be a function and let $x \in X$.
Neighbourhoods are as in [[def-neighbourhood-top]].

$f$ is **continuous at $x$** if for every neighbourhood $V$ of $f(x)$ in $Y$ the
preimage $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$ in $X$.

$f$ is **continuous** if it is continuous at every point of $X$.

**The same condition with open sets only.** $f$ is continuous at $x$ if and only
if for every open $V \subseteq Y$ with $f(x) \in V$ there is an open
$U \subseteq X$ with $x \in U$ and $f[U] \subseteq V$. Indeed, if $f$ is
continuous at $x$ and $V$ is such an open set, then $V$ is a neighbourhood of
$f(x)$, so $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$ and contains an open $U \ni x$,
which satisfies $f[U] \subseteq V$. Conversely, given the displayed condition and
a neighbourhood $V$ of $f(x)$, fix open $V_0$ with $f(x) \in V_0 \subseteq V$ and
then open $U \ni x$ with $f[U] \subseteq V_0$; then $x \in U \subseteq f^{-1}[V_0] \subseteq f^{-1}[V]$,
so $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$. Both forms are used below and are the
same statement written twice.

**Preimage, not image.** $f^{-1}[V] = \{\, x \in X : f(x) \in V \,\}$
is the preimage in the sense of [[def-injection-surjection-bijection]] and is
defined for every function, invertible or not; no inverse function is being
asserted to exist. Continuity is a condition on preimages throughout, and the
corresponding conditions on images define the *open* and *closed* maps of a later
item, which are different notions.

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

derivations.claim: (Spectral representation and the bounds (a).) By [L1] choose an orthonormal basis $e_1,\dots,e_m$ of $\mathbb R^m$ with $Be_i=\lambda_ie_i$ and real $\lambda_i$. Writing $z=\sum_iz_ie_i$ gives $z^{\mathsf T}Bz=\sum_i\lambda_iz_i^2$ and $|z|^2=\sum_iz_i^2$. If some $\lambda_i\le0$, then $e_i^{\mathsf T}Be_i=\lambda_i\le0$ with $e_i\ne0$, contradicting positive definiteness; so all $\lambda_i>0$. Put $a:=\min_i\lambda_i$ and $b:=\max_i\lambda_i$; both are positive and $a|z|^2\le z^{\mathsf T}Bz\le b|z|^2$ follows from the representation. This is (a).

(Uniform bounds on a compact parameter set (c).) The function $\Phi(\lambda,z):=z^{\mathsf T}B(\lambda)z$ is continuous on the compact metric space $\Lambda\times S^{m-1}$, where $S^{m-1}:=\{z:|z|=1\}$; by [L3] it attains a minimum $a$ and a maximum $b$. At every point of the compact product one has $\Phi>0$ because $B(\lambda)$ is positive definite and $z\ne0$; hence $a>0$, and every $z\ne0$ can be written as $|z|\,\hat z$ with $\hat z\in S^{m-1}$, giving $a|z|^2\le z^{\mathsf T}B(\lambda)z\le b|z|^2$.

(Inverse bounds (b).) In the same eigenbasis, $B^{-1}e_i=\lambda_i^{-1}e_i$ and $\lambda_i^{-1}\in[b^{-1},a^{-1}]$, so $b^{-1}|z|^2\le z^{\mathsf T}B^{-1}z\le a^{-1}|z|^2$; in particular $B^{-1}$ exists.

(Smoothness of the inverse (d).) On $D$, $x\mapsto\det B(x)\ge a^m>0$: the determinant is the product of the eigenvalues, each at least $a$ by (a) applied at $x$, or equivalently $\det$ is continuous and positive. The adjugate entries are polynomial in the entries of $B$, hence smooth in $x$, and dividing by the smooth nonzero function $\det B$ is smooth by [L4]; so $B(x)^{-1}$ is smooth and satisfies the bound by (b).

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]) for the quotient, product-measure and integration
clauses below, as in [[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]].

**(a) The 2 pi-periodic torus.** Let $\mathbb T_{2\pi}:=\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z$
carry the quotient topology, and let
$$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}:=\mathbb T_{2\pi}\times\mathbb T_{2\pi}\times\mathbb T_{2\pi}$$
with the product topology; write $q:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ for the
quotient map and $[x]:=(x^1+2\pi\mathbb Z,x^2+2\pi\mathbb Z,x^3+2\pi\mathbb Z)$.
The map $[0,2\pi)^3\to\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, $x\mapsto[x]$, is a bijection. The
normalized product measure $\mu$ is $\mu_{\mathbb T}\otimes\mu_{\mathbb T}\otimes\mu_{\mathbb T}$,
where $\mu_{\mathbb T}$ is the normalized measure of
[[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]] transported by
$t\mapsto2\pi t$; it is a probability measure on the Borel sets of
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ and $\int f\,d\mu=(2\pi)^{-3}\int_{[0,2\pi)^3}f\circ q\,d\lambda_3$
for bounded measurable $f$ ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

**(b) Test functions and continuous classes.** For $N\ge1$ let
$C^\infty(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the set of compositions
$u\circ q$ of smooth maps $u:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^N$ that are $2\pi$-periodic
in each variable; these are the **smooth test functions** (real-valued when
$N=1$). For $m\ge0$ let $C^m(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the set of
$u\circ q$ with $u\in C^m(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^N)$ $2\pi$-periodic in each
variable ([[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]), with
$$\|u\|_{C^m}:=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\ \sup_{x\in\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}\bigl|(D^\alpha u)(x)\bigr| ,$$
where $D^\alpha$ is the multi-index derivative of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]] applied to any
periodic representative; the displayed expression is independent of the
representative.

**(c) The Hilbert space $L^2$.** For $N\ge1$ let
$L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the quotient of the set of measurable
$u$ with $\int|u|^2\,d\mu<\infty$ by the $\mu$-a.e. zero functions
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]),
with inner product $\langle u,v\rangle_2=\int u\cdot v\,d\mu$ and norm
$\|u\|_2=\langle u,u\rangle_2^{1/2}$; it is a real Hilbert space
([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]). For
$u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ and $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ the
**$k$-th Fourier coefficient** is the vector
$$\widehat u(k):=\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}u(x)\,e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)\in\mathbb C^N ,$$
where $e^{-ik\cdot x}:=\chi_{-k}$ with $\chi_k([x]):=\exp(i\,k\cdot x)$; here
$u$ is read through any representative. Write $\chi_k:\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\to\mathbb C$,
$k\in\mathbb Z^3$, for these **characters**; under the identification
$x=2\pi y$ they are the characters $\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot y)$ of
[[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]], so $(\chi_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}$
is an orthonormal basis of the complex space $L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb C)$.

**(d) Weak derivatives and the periodic Sobolev spaces.** For
$u,v\in L^1(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R)$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^3$ say that
$v$ is the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}v\,\varphi\,d\mu$$
for every $\varphi\in C^\infty(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R)$, where $D^\alpha\varphi$
is the multi-index derivative of the periodic representative
([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]] records the
Euclidean analogue). For an integer $s\ge0$ let
$$H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N):=\Bigl\{u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N):\ \text{for every }|\alpha|\le s\text{ there is }v_\alpha\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)\text{ with }v_\alpha=D^\alpha u\Bigr\},$$
the vector-valued weak derivative being componentwise, and put
$$\|u\|_{H^s}:=\Bigl(\sum_{|\alpha|\le s}\|D^\alpha u\|_2^2\Bigr)^{1/2}.$$
The classes $L^2\subseteq L^1$ on the probability space, so the integrals in the
test identity are finite: $|\int u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu|\le\|u\|_2\|D^\alpha\varphi\|_2$
by Cauchy--Schwarz. The definition asserts neither that the weak derivative
exists nor that the two norms compared in the next item are equivalent; those
are proved in [[lem-gr-periodic-fourier-differentiation-and-norm-equivalence]].

**(e) Conventions.** $O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ open, $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ an
interval and maps $F:I\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\times O\to\mathbb R^{m'}$ are
called smooth when their representatives $F(t,q(x),u)=G(t,x,u)$ have
$G\in C^\infty$. Throughout this page the torus is always this
$2\pi$-periodic one; a statement "for every $x$" means for every point of
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, and "a.e." means $\mu$-a.e.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$

**(c) The Hilbert space $L^2$.** For $N\ge1$ let
$L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the quotient of the set of measurable
$u$ with $\int|u|^2\,d\mu<\infty$ by the $\mu$-a.e. zero functions
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]),
with inner product $\langle u,v\rangle_2=\int u\cdot v\,d\mu$ and norm
$\|u\|_2=\langle u,u\rangle_2^{1/2}$; it is a real Hilbert space
([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]). For
$u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ and $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ the
**$k$-th Fourier coefficient** is the vector
$$\widehat u(k):=\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}u(x)\,e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)\in\mathbb C^N ,$$
where $e^{-ik\cdot x}:=\chi_{-k}$ with $\chi_k([x]):=\exp(i\,k\cdot x)$; here
$u$ is read through any representative. Write $\chi_k:\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\to\mathbb C$,
$k\in\mathbb Z^3$, for these **characters**; under the identification
$x=2\pi y$ they are the characters $\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot y)$ of
[[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]], so $(\chi_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}$
is an orthonormal basis of the complex space $L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb C)$.

**(d) Weak derivatives and the periodic Sobolev spaces.** For
$u,v\in L^1(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R)$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^3$ say that
$v$ is the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}v\,\varphi\,d\mu$$
for every $\varphi\in C^\infty(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R)$, where $D^\alpha\varphi$
is the multi-index derivative of the periodic representative
([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]] records the
Euclidean analogue). For an integer $s\ge0$ let
$$H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N):=\Bigl\{u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N):\ \text{for every }|\alpha|\le s\text{ there is }v_\alpha\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)\text{ with }v_\alpha=D^\alpha u\Bigr\},$$
the vector-valued weak derivative being componentwise, and put
$$\|u\|_{H^s}:=\Bigl(\sum_{|\alpha|\le s}\|D^\alpha u\|_2^2\Bigr)^{1/2}.$$
The classes $L^2\subseteq L^1$ on the probability space, so the integrals in the
test identity are finite: $|\int u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu|\le\|u\|_2\|D^\alpha\varphi\|_2$
by Cauchy--Schwarz. The definition asserts neither that the weak derivative
exists nor that the two norms compared in the next item are equivalent; those
are proved in [[lem-gr-periodic-fourier-differentiation-and-norm-equivalence]].

**(e) Conventions.** $O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ open, $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ an
interval and maps $F:I\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\times O\to\mathbb R^{m'}$ are
called smooth when their representatives $F(t,q(x),u)=G(t,x,u)$ have
$G\in C^\infty$. Throughout this page the torus is always this
$2\pi$-periodic one; a statement "for every $x$" means for every point of
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, and "a.e." means $\mu$-a.e.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $k \in \mathcal{W}(n,m)$, that is
$k : m \to \mathbb{N}$ with $\sum_{i<m}k_i = n$
([[def-multinomial-coefficient]]). Then:

1. **The closed formula, in $\mathbb{N}$.**
   $$\binom{n}{k}\cdot\prod_{i<m} k_i! \;=\; n! ,$$
   so in $\mathbb{R}$ the quotient $\iota(n!)\big/\prod_{i<m}\iota(k_i!)$ is
   $\iota\binom{n}{k}$, the canonical natural of a count.
2. **The expansion, in $\mathbb{R}$.** For $x : m \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $$\Big(\sum_{i<m} x_i\Big)^{n} \;=\; \sum_{k \in \mathcal{W}(n,m)} \iota\binom{n}{k}\prod_{i<m} x_i^{\,k_i},$$
   the outer sum being the sum over the finite index set $\mathcal{W}(n,m)$
   ([[def-sum-over-a-finite-index-set]]) and the inner product the real finite
   product of [[def-finite-sum]].

As with the binomial theorem, the identity is stated in $\mathbb{R}$; the
commutative-ring version is a separate statement, to be made where rings exist.
See the Remarks of [[thm-binomial-theorem]].

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

derivations.claim: (One-variable periodic integration by parts.) For smooth $2\pi$-periodic $G,H$ and each $j$, $\int_{\mathbb T_{2\pi}}G\,\partial_jH\,d\mu_{\mathbb T}=-\int_{\mathbb T_{2\pi}}(\partial_jG)\,H\,d\mu_{\mathbb T}$: indeed $\int_0^{2\pi}\partial_j(GH)\,dx_j=(GH)|_0^{2\pi}=0$ by the second fundamental theorem of calculus and periodicity [L3], and the product rule gives the claim; the remaining coordinates integrate out by the product-measure convention. Consequently, for every smooth $\varphi$, every $k$ and every $\alpha$, $\int \chi_kD^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu=(-1)^{|\alpha|}(ik)^\alpha\int\chi_k\varphi\,d\mu$: induct on $|\alpha|$, moving one variable derivative from $\varphi$ onto $\chi_k$ by the one-variable identity and using $\partial_j\chi_k=ik_j\chi_k$. In particular $D^\alpha\chi_k=(ik)^\alpha\chi_k$ in the weak sense of [L2], the case $\varphi=\chi_{-l}$ tested against $\chi_k$ having Fourier coefficients $\widehat{\chi_k}(l)=\delta_{kl}$.

(The symbol bounds.) For $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ put $q_k:=\sum_{|\alpha|\le s}|k^\alpha|^2$, where $k^\alpha=k_1^{\alpha_1}k_2^{\alpha_2}k_3^{\alpha_3}$. Then $q_k\le(s+1)^3(1+|k|^2)^s$, because $|k^\alpha|^2\le(1+|k|^2)^{|\alpha|}\le(1+|k|^2)^s$ for $|\alpha|\le s$ and there are at most $(s+1)^3$ multi-indices in the range. Conversely $(1+|k|^2)^s\le2^s(1+|k|^{2s})$, and by the multinomial expansion [L4] with $x_j=|k_j|^2$ one has $|k|^{2s}=\sum_{|\alpha|=s}\frac{s!}{\alpha!}|k^\alpha|^2\ge\sum_{|\alpha|=s}|k^\alpha|^2$; hence $(1+|k|^2)^s\le2^s(1+q_k)\le2^{s+1}q_k$, because $q_k\ge1$ (the term $\alpha=0$ equals $1$). Thus $2^{-(s+1)}(1+|k|^2)^s\le q_k\le(s+1)^3(1+|k|^2)^s$.

(The differentiation identity (a).) If $u\in H^s$ and $|\alpha|\le s$, then $D^\alpha u\in H^{s-|\alpha|}$: a weak derivative of $D^\alpha u$ of order $|\beta|\le s-|\alpha|$ is the weak derivative $D^{\alpha+\beta}u$, because the defining test identity for the iterated derivative follows by applying the two defining identities in succession and noting that $D^\beta\varphi$ is again a smooth test function. Testing the defining identity for $D^\alpha u$ against $\varphi=\chi_{-k}$ gives $\widehat{D^\alpha u}(k)=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int u\,D^\alpha\chi_{-k}\,d\mu=(-1)^{|\alpha|}(-ik)^\alpha\int u\,\chi_{-k}\,d\mu=(ik)^\alpha\widehat u(k)$, where the middle equality uses step 1.1 for the smooth test function $D^\alpha\chi_{-k}=(-ik)^\alpha\chi_{-k}$ and the last uses $(-1)^{|\alpha|}(-i)^\alpha=i^\alpha$.

(The norm bounds for $u\in H^s$.) By Parseval [L1] applied to the $L^2$ classes $D^\alpha u$, $\|D^\alpha u\|_2^2=\sum_k|k^\alpha|^2|\widehat u(k)|^2$, so the definition of the $H^s$ norm gives $\|u\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_kq_k|\widehat u(k)|^2$. Combining with step 1.2, $\|u\|_{H^s}^2\le(s+1)^3N_s(u)^2$ and $N_s(u)^2\le2^{s+1}\|u\|_{H^s}^2$, which are the right-hand inequality and the converse inequality of (b) whenever $u\in H^s$.

(Converse direction of (b): the weighted series produce weak derivatives.) Let $u\in L^2$ with $N_s(u)<\infty$. For each $|\alpha|\le s$ the sequence $k\mapsto(ik)^\alpha\widehat u(k)$ is square-summable because $|k^\alpha|^2\le(1+|k|^2)^{|\alpha|}\le(1+|k|^2)^s$; by the surjectivity of the coefficient isometry [L1] there is a unique class $w_\alpha\in L^2$ with $\widehat{w_\alpha}(k)=(ik)^\alpha\widehat u(k)$. For a smooth real test $\varphi$, Parseval's pairing identity [L1] gives $\int u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu=\sum_k\widehat u(k)\overline{\widehat{D^\alpha\varphi}(k)}=\sum_k\widehat u(k)\overline{(ik)^\alpha\widehat\varphi(k)}=\sum_k(-1)^{|\alpha|}(ik)^\alpha\widehat u(k)\overline{\widehat\varphi(k)}=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int w_\alpha\varphi\,d\mu$, where the second equality is step 2.1 applied to the smooth $\varphi$ and the third uses $\overline{(ik)^\alpha}=(-i)^\alpha k^\alpha=(-1)^{|\alpha|}(ik)^\alpha$. Hence $D^\alpha u=w_\alpha$ weakly for every $|\alpha|\le s$, so $u\in H^s$.

(Conclusion.) By step 3.1 and step 2.2, for $u$ with $N_s(u)<\infty$ the class lies in $H^s$ and satisfies $2^{-(s+1)}N_s(u)^2\le\|u\|_{H^s}^2\le(s+1)^3N_s(u)^2$, so (b) holds with $c_s=2^{-(s+1)}$ and $C_s=(s+1)^3$, while (a) was proved in step 2.1.

boundaries.reason: No empty set, empty family or empty index range is formed: the quantified objects (points, fields, mode families, data sets) are nonempty by the hypotheses, and the proofs never split off an empty case.
The value zero is not a distinguished boundary of this claim: no step divides by a quantity that can vanish and no separate zero case is required.
No cardinality-one case is separated: the arguments treat general finite or countable families and the one-element case is included without special treatment.

The hypotheses exclude degenerate configurations: the metric is Lorentzian/nondegenerate, the time matrix or coefficient is positive definite, velocity fields are unit and nonzero where required, and no degenerate limit is claimed.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, $\mu$, $\chi_k$,
$\widehat u(k)$, the weak derivatives $D^\alpha$ and the spaces
$H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be as in
[[def-gr-periodic-torus-and-sobolev-spaces]], and put
$$N_s(u)^2:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+|k|^2)^s\,|\widehat u(k)|^2,\qquad |k|^2:=k_1^2+k_2^2+k_3^2 .$$

**(a)** Let $u\in H^s$ and let $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^3$ with $|\alpha|\le s$. Then
$D^\alpha u\in H^{s-|\alpha|}$ and
$$\widehat{D^\alpha u}(k)=(ik)^\alpha\,\widehat u(k)\qquad(k\in\mathbb Z^3),\qquad (ik)^\alpha:=\prod_{j=1}^3(ik_j)^{\alpha_j}.$$

**(b)** Let $u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ satisfy $N_s(u)<\infty$.
Then $u\in H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$, and there are constants
$0<c_s\le C_s<\infty$, depending only on $s$, such that
$$c_s\,N_s(u)^2\le\|u\|_{H^s}^2\le C_s\,N_s(u)^2 .$$
The right-hand inequality holds for every $u\in H^s$, so the two norms are
equivalent on $H^s$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]) for the quotient, product-measure and integration
clauses below, as in [[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]].

**(a) The 2 pi-periodic torus.** Let $\mathbb T_{2\pi}:=\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z$
carry the quotient topology, and let
$$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}:=\mathbb T_{2\pi}\times\mathbb T_{2\pi}\times\mathbb T_{2\pi}$$
with the product topology; write $q:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ for the
quotient map and $[x]:=(x^1+2\pi\mathbb Z,x^2+2\pi\mathbb Z,x^3+2\pi\mathbb Z)$.
The map $[0,2\pi)^3\to\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, $x\mapsto[x]$, is a bijection. The
normalized product measure $\mu$ is $\mu_{\mathbb T}\otimes\mu_{\mathbb T}\otimes\mu_{\mathbb T}$,
where $\mu_{\mathbb T}$ is the normalized measure of
[[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]] transported by
$t\mapsto2\pi t$; it is a probability measure on the Borel sets of
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ and $\int f\,d\mu=(2\pi)^{-3}\int_{[0,2\pi)^3}f\circ q\,d\lambda_3$
for bounded measurable $f$ ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

**(b) Test functions and continuous classes.** For $N\ge1$ let
$C^\infty(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the set of compositions
$u\circ q$ of smooth maps $u:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^N$ that are $2\pi$-periodic
in each variable; these are the **smooth test functions** (real-valued when
$N=1$). For $m\ge0$ let $C^m(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the set of
$u\circ q$ with $u\in C^m(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^N)$ $2\pi$-periodic in each
variable ([[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]), with
$$\|u\|_{C^m}:=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\ \sup_{x\in\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}\bigl|(D^\alpha u)(x)\bigr| ,$$
where $D^\alpha$ is the multi-index derivative of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]] applied to any
periodic representative; the displayed expression is independent of the
representative.

**(c) The Hilbert space $L^2$.** For $N\ge1$ let
$L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the quotient of the set of measurable
$u$ with $\int|u|^2\,d\mu<\infty$ by the $\mu$-a.e. zero functions
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]),
with inner product $\langle u,v\rangle_2=\int u\cdot v\,d\mu$ and norm
$\|u\|_2=\langle u,u\rangle_2^{1/2}$; it is a real Hilbert space
([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]). For
$u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ and $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ the
**$k$-th Fourier coefficient** is the vector
$$\widehat u(k):=\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}u(x)\,e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)\in\mathbb C^N ,$$
where $e^{-ik\cdot x}:=\chi_{-k}$ with $\chi_k([x]):=\exp(i\,k\cdot x)$; here
$u$ is read through any representative. Write $\chi_k:\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\to\mathbb C$,
$k\in\mathbb Z^3$, for these **characters**; under the identification
$x=2\pi y$ they are the characters $\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot y)$ of
[[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]], so $(\chi_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}$
is an orthonormal basis of the complex space $L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb C)$.

**(d) Weak derivatives and the periodic Sobolev spaces.** For
$u,v\in L^1(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R)$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^3$ say that
$v$ is the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}v\,\varphi\,d\mu$$
for every $\varphi\in C^\infty(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R)$, where $D^\alpha\varphi$
is the multi-index derivative of the periodic representative
([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]] records the
Euclidean analogue). For an integer $s\ge0$ let
$$H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N):=\Bigl\{u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N):\ \text{for every }|\alpha|\le s\text{ there is }v_\alpha\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)\text{ with }v_\alpha=D^\alpha u\Bigr\},$$
the vector-valued weak derivative being componentwise, and put
$$\|u\|_{H^s}:=\Bigl(\sum_{|\alpha|\le s}\|D^\alpha u\|_2^2\Bigr)^{1/2}.$$
The classes $L^2\subseteq L^1$ on the probability space, so the integrals in the
test identity are finite: $|\int u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu|\le\|u\|_2\|D^\alpha\varphi\|_2$
by Cauchy--Schwarz. The definition asserts neither that the weak derivative
exists nor that the two norms compared in the next item are equivalent; those
are proved in [[lem-gr-periodic-fourier-differentiation-and-norm-equivalence]].

**(e) Conventions.** $O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ open, $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ an
interval and maps $F:I\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\times O\to\mathbb R^{m'}$ are
called smooth when their representatives $F(t,q(x),u)=G(t,x,u)$ have
$G\in C^\infty$. Throughout this page the torus is always this
$2\pi$-periodic one; a statement "for every $x$" means for every point of
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, and "a.e." means $\mu$-a.e.

Throughout, $\mathbb F$ is $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ and families are indexed by
an arbitrary set $I$, with no enumeration or countability assumed. Finite real lists use [[def-finite-sum]], and sums over finite subsets use [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] in the additive monoid of the scalar field. Disjoint splitting is [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]], and scalar modulus estimates use [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]; all suprema and infima of real sets below are
taken in the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) or in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]], [[lem-extended-reals-complete]]).

**Sums of nonnegative families.** Let $(c_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of
nonnegative reals and let $\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ be the set of finite subsets of
$I$, ordered by inclusion. Define

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i:=\sup\Bigl\{\sum_{i\in F}c_i \;:\; F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)\Bigr\}\in[0,+\infty] .$$

The set of finite subsums is nonempty, since $\varnothing$ contributes the empty
sum $0$, so the supremum exists in $[0,+\infty]$; it is a real number exactly
when the finite subsums are bounded above in $\mathbb R$, and $+\infty$
otherwise. For finite $I$ the finite subsum at $I$ is the largest of all finite
subsums, because all terms are nonnegative, so the definition agrees with the
finite sum; in particular $\sum_{i\in I}c_i=0$ when every $c_i$ is $0$, and
$I=\varnothing$ gives the empty sum $0$.

**Splitting identity and small tails.** Fix a finite $F\subseteq I$. Every
finite $G\subseteq I$ splits as the disjoint union $(G\cap F)\cup(G\setminus F)$,
so $\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in G\cap F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i\le\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i$;
conversely the finite $G$ with $F\subseteq G$ satisfy
$\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i$. Taking suprema,
with the constant $\sum_{i\in F}c_i$ passing through the supremum,

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i . \qquad (1)$$

Consequently, if $S:=\sum_{i\in I}c_i$ is finite, then for every real
$\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite $F\subseteq I$ with
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i<\varepsilon$: the finite subsums form a nonempty
bounded-above set with supremum $S$, so by the epsilon characterisation of the
supremum ([[lem-sup-epsilon]]) some finite $F$ has
$S-\varepsilon<\sum_{i\in F}c_i$, and (1) gives
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i=S-\sum_{i\in F}c_i<\varepsilon$. Such an $F$ is
called a **tail-control set** for $\varepsilon$.

**Sums of scalar families.** Now let $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family in $\mathbb F$
and put $s_F:=\sum_{i\in F}a_i$ for finite $F\subseteq I$. The set
$\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ with inclusion is a directed preorder: it is nonempty and
$F\cup G$ is a common upper bound of $F$ and $G$
([[def-directed-set-and-net]]). Hence $(s_F)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$ is a
net in $\mathbb F$, the **finite-subset net** of the family, and the family is
**summable** when this net converges
([[def-net-convergence-and-cluster-point]]). The scalar metric is the usual real metric or [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. These metric spaces are Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]]. A net in $\mathbb F$ has at most one limit
([[thm-hausdorff-iff-net-limits-are-unique]]), so for a summable family the
limit is unique and we write $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\lim_F s_F$ for it. The family is
**absolutely summable** when $\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|<+\infty$ in the sense above.

**Every absolutely summable family is summable, in ZF.** Assume
$S:=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|$ is finite and put $S_F:=\sum_{i\in F}|a_i|$ for finite
$F$. For finite $F,G\subseteq I$ the triangle inequality for finite sums and the
fact that a finite subsum is at most the whole nonnegative sum give

$$|s_F-s_G|\le\sum_{i\in F\triangle G}|a_i|\le S-S_{F\cap G} . \qquad (2)$$

Now fix a real $\varepsilon>0$, let $F_0$ be a tail-control set for
$\varepsilon$, and let $F,G\supseteq F_0$ be finite. Then $F\cap G\supseteq F_0$,
so $S-S_{F\cap G}\le S-S_{F_0}<\varepsilon$ and (2) gives
$|s_F-s_G|<\varepsilon$.

First suppose $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$. For each finite $F$ define
$A_F:=\inf\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ and $B_F:=\sup\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ over
finite $G$. Both are real numbers, because $|s_G|\le S_G\le S$, so the two sets
are nonempty and bounded, and $A_F\le B_F$. If $H\supseteq F$ then
$A_H\ge A_F$ and $B_H\le B_F$. Let $L:=\sup_FA_F$ and $U:=\inf_FB_F$.
Since $A_F\le s_{F\cup H}\le B_H$ for all finite $F,H$, we get $L\le U$.
Moreover, the preceding estimate holds for every pair $F,G\supseteq F_0$;
taking the supremum over $F$ and the infimum over $G$ gives
$B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$. Hence
$0\le U-L\le B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so
$L=U=:s$. If $F\supseteq F_0$, then both $s_F$ and $s$ lie in
$[A_{F_0},B_{F_0}]$, and therefore $|s_F-s|\le\varepsilon$.

If $\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, apply the real argument just proved to the families
$(\operatorname{Re}a_i)$ and $(\operatorname{Im}a_i)$. They are absolutely
summable because $|\operatorname{Re}a_i|,|\operatorname{Im}a_i|\le|a_i|$.
Their finite-subset nets converge to real numbers $r$ and $t$, respectively,
so $s_F\to r+it$ in $\mathbb C$. Thus every absolutely summable real or complex
family is summable. **No choice principle is used**: the construction uses only
two-sided suprema in $\mathbb R$.

**Linearity and absolute value.** If $(a_i)$ and $(b_i)$ are absolutely
summable and $\lambda\in\mathbb F$, then so are $(a_i+b_i)$ and
$(\lambda a_i)$, and

$$\sum_{i\in I}(a_i+b_i)=\sum_{i\in I}a_i+\sum_{i\in I}b_i,\qquad \sum_{i\in I}\lambda a_i=\lambda\sum_{i\in I}a_i,\qquad \Bigl|\sum_{i\in I}a_i\Bigr|\le\sum_{i\in I}|a_i| ,$$

because the corresponding identities hold for every finite subsum, both sides
are limits of the corresponding finite-subset nets, and addition, scalar
multiplication and the modulus are continuous. The splitting identity (1)
likewise passes to absolutely summable scalar families:
$\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{i\in F}a_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}a_i$ for every finite
$F$, because finite subsums over sets containing $F$ converge to the left-hand
side and equal the finite sum over $F$ plus the finite subsum of the tail, whose
net converges to the tail sum.

**The finite-dimensional Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.** Let $(u_k)_{0\le k<m}$ and $(v_k)_{0\le k<m}$ be scalar lists, for $m\in\mathbb N$ and let $t\in\mathbb R$. Every term of
$\sum_{k<m}(|u_k|-t|v_k|)^2$ is nonnegative, so for all real $t$

$$0\le\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2-2t\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|+t^2\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2 .$$

If $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2>0$, substituting
$t=\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)/\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$ gives
$\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)^2\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$;
if $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2=0$ then every $v_k=0$ and both sides are $0$. In either case
$\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$
after taking square roots, and applying the modulus inequality for finite sums
to $u_k\overline{v_k}$ also gives

$$\Bigl|\sum_{k<m}u_k\overline{v_k}\Bigr|\le\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2} . \qquad (3)$$

**The space $\ell^2(I)$.** For a family $a=(a_i)_{i\in I}$ in $\mathbb F$ define
$Q(a):=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|^2$. If $Q(a)$ is finite, set $\|a\|_2:=\sqrt{Q(a)}$, using the nonnegative real square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]]; if $Q(a)=+\infty$, set $\|a\|_2:=+\infty$. This is a case definition, not exponentiation of an extended real. Let

$$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F):=\{\,a=(a_i)_{i\in I} : \|a\|_2<+\infty\,\}.$$

The set $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is a vector space over $\mathbb F$: it contains the
zero family, is closed under scalar multiplication because
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$, and is closed under addition because (3)
applied to finite subsums gives $\|a+b\|_2\le\|a\|_2+\|b\|_2<+\infty$. The same
inequality is the triangle inequality for $\|\cdot\|_2$, which is moreover
nonnegative, vanishes only for the zero family (an arbitrary sum of nonnegative
terms with supremum $0$ has every term $0$) and satisfies
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$; thus $\|\cdot\|_2$ is a norm on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$. Finally the **pairing**
$\langle a,b\rangle:=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\overline{b_i}$ is well defined on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)\times\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$, because
$|a_i\overline{b_i}|=|a_i||b_i|$ has finite nonnegative sum by (3); it is linear
in the first variable, conjugate symmetric, positive definite, and satisfies
$\langle a,a\rangle=\|a\|_2^2$, all by the corresponding finite identities and
the linearity of the sum. Consequently $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is an inner-product
space, and $e_i\in\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ denotes the family that is $1$ at $i$ and
$0$ elsewhere. **Nothing here asserts that $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is complete**;
that follows later, from an orthonormal basis of a Hilbert space.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

For $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C^n$, the formulas

$$\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathbb R^n}=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k,\qquad \langle z,w\rangle_{\mathbb C^n}=\sum_{k<n}z_k\overline{w_k}$$

define inner products, linear in the first argument. At $n=0$, the unique pairing on the zero space is an inner product.

Let $a<b$ be reals and let $f_k:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuously
differentiable: each $f_k$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$ and each derivative
$f_k'$ is continuous there ([[def-continuity-real]]). Suppose there is
$c\in[a,b]$ such that the real
sequence $(f_k(c))$ converges to $A$, and suppose $f_k'\to g$ uniformly on
$[a,b]$. Then there is a differentiable function $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ such
that

$$f_k\longrightarrow f\ \text{ uniformly},\qquad f'=g.$$

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space. If continuous functions $f_n:X\to\mathbb C$ converge uniformly to $f:X\to\mathbb C$ in the sense of [[def-uniform-convergence-of-complex-valued-functions]], then $f$ is continuous.

derivations.claim: (Absolute convergence of the differentiated coefficient series.) Fix $|\alpha|\le m$ and put $\theta_\alpha:=s-|\alpha|\ge s-m>3/2$. For every finite $F\subseteq\mathbb Z^3$, Cauchy--Schwarz [L4] with $a_k:=|k^\alpha|$ and $b_k:=|k^\alpha||\widehat u(k)|$ gives $\sum_{k\in F}|k^\alpha||\widehat u(k)|\le\bigl(\sum_{k\in F}|k^\alpha|^2(1+|k|^2)^{-\theta_\alpha}\bigr)^{1/2}\bigl(\sum_{k\in F}(1+|k|^2)^{\theta_\alpha}|\widehat u(k)|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$; passing to the supremum over finite $F$ by [L3] and using $|k^\alpha|^2\le(1+|k|^2)^{|\alpha|}$, and $\theta_\alpha+|\alpha|=s$, yields $\sum_k|k^\alpha||\widehat u(k)|\le\bigl(\sum_k(1+|k|^2)^{-(s-m)}\bigr)^{1/2}N_s(u)$.

(The weight sum is finite.) For $\theta>3/2$, $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+|k|^2)^{-\theta}<+\infty$: the ball $|k|\le1$ contributes at most $27$ terms, and the dyadic shell $2^j\le|k|<2^{j+1}$ ($j\ge0$) contains at most $C_3 2^{3j}$ lattice points each weighted by at most $2^{-2j\theta}$, so the shell sum is at most $C_3 2^{-j(2\theta-3)}$ and $\sum_j2^{-j(2\theta-3)}<\infty$ by the geometric series. Hence with $\theta:=s-m$ step 1.1 gives $\sum_k|k^\alpha||\widehat u(k)|\le C_{s,m}N_s(u)\le C'_{s,m}\|u\|_{H^s}$ by [L1].

(The limit series gives a $C^m$ representative.) For finite $F$ put $S_F:=\sum_{k\in F}\widehat u(k)\chi_k$, a $C^\infty$ function. If $F,G$ are finite then $\|S_F-S_G\|_{C^m}\le\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sum_{k\in F\triangle G}|k^\alpha||\widehat u(k)|$, and the tail sums tend to zero along the finite-subset net by [L3] and step 2.1; hence the derivative series for every $|\alpha|\le m$ satisfies the uniform Cauchy property on $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$. Applying the interval differentiation theorem [L5] successively along each coordinate direction and for each order gives a $C^m$ function $u^*$ with $D^\alpha u^*=\sum_k(ik)^\alpha\widehat u(k)\chi_k$ for every $|\alpha|\le m$, the series converging absolutely and uniformly by step 2.1; and $\|u^*\|_{C^m}\le C\|u\|_{H^s}$ by step 2.1. Since $S_F\to u$ in $L^2$ by [L2] and $S_F\to u^*$ uniformly, $u^*$ represents the class $u$; two continuous representatives of one $L^2$ class agree everywhere, giving uniqueness. This proves (a).

(The Hölder modulus (b).) For $x,y$ and $|\alpha|\le m$, $|D^\alpha u^*(x)-D^\alpha u^*(y)|\le\sum_k|k^\alpha||\widehat u(k)|\,|\chi_k(x)-\chi_k(y)|\le\sum_k|k^\alpha||\widehat u(k)|\min\{2,|k|d(x,y)\}$ by [L6]. For $0<\theta\le1$ one has $\min\{2,t\}\le2^{1-\theta}t^\theta$ for every $t\ge0$ (for $t\le2$ because $2^{1-\theta}t^\theta\ge t$ iff $2\ge t$; for $t\ge2$ because $t^\theta\ge2^\theta$), so the sum is at most $2^{1-\theta}d(x,y)^\theta\sum_k|k|^{m+\theta}|\widehat u(k)|\le C_\theta d(x,y)^\theta\|u\|_{H^s}$ by steps 1.1 and 2.1 applied with exponent $s-(m+\theta)>3/2$, valid for $\theta<s-m-3/2$; for the endpoint value $\theta_0=\min\{1,s-m-3/2\}$ choose $\theta<\theta_0$ and use $d(x,y)^{\theta_0}\ge \operatorname{diam}(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi})^{\theta_0-\theta}d(x,y)^\theta$. This proves (b).

(Linearity and convergence (c).) $D^\alpha$ is linear and the series representation is linear in the coefficients, so $u\mapsto u^*$ is linear; and for $u_j\to u$ in $H^s$, applying (a) to the difference gives $\|u_j^*-u^*\|_{C^m}\le C\|u_j-u\|_{H^s}\to0$, which is uniform convergence of all derivatives of order at most $m$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, $\mu$, $\chi_k$,
$\widehat u(k)$, the weak derivatives $D^\alpha$ and the spaces
$H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be as in
[[def-gr-periodic-torus-and-sobolev-spaces]], and put
$$N_s(u)^2:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+|k|^2)^s\,|\widehat u(k)|^2,\qquad |k|^2:=k_1^2+k_2^2+k_3^2 .$$

**(a)** Let $u\in H^s$ and let $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^3$ with $|\alpha|\le s$. Then
$D^\alpha u\in H^{s-|\alpha|}$ and
$$\widehat{D^\alpha u}(k)=(ik)^\alpha\,\widehat u(k)\qquad(k\in\mathbb Z^3),\qquad (ik)^\alpha:=\prod_{j=1}^3(ik_j)^{\alpha_j}.$$

**(b)** Let $u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ satisfy $N_s(u)<\infty$.
Then $u\in H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$, and there are constants
$0<c_s\le C_s<\infty$, depending only on $s$, such that
$$c_s\,N_s(u)^2\le\|u\|_{H^s}^2\le C_s\,N_s(u)^2 .$$
The right-hand inequality holds for every $u\in H^s$, so the two norms are
equivalent on $H^s$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, $\mu$, $\chi_k$ and the
spaces $H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^m)$ be as in
[[def-gr-periodic-torus-and-sobolev-spaces]] ($m\ge1$).

**(a) Mode sets.** For $N\ge0$ put
$\Lambda_N:=\{k\in\mathbb Z^3:|k|\le N\}$ with $|k|$ the Euclidean norm, and
$$X_N:=\Bigl\{\sum_{k\in\Lambda_N}a_k\chi_k:\ a_k\in\mathbb C^m,\ a_{-k}=\overline{a_k}\Bigr\}\subseteq C^\infty(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^m),$$
the **Galerkin space of modes up to $N$**; it is a finite-dimensional real
vector space of dimension $d_N:=m\,|\Lambda_N|$, and $X_N\subseteq X_{N'}$ for
$N\le N'$. (The reality condition $a_{-k}=\overline{a_k}$ is exactly the
condition that the trigonometric polynomial be real-valued.)

**(b) Projection.** For $u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^m)$ define
$$P_Nu:=\sum_{k\in\Lambda_N}\widehat u(k)\chi_k,\qquad (P_Nu)(x)=\sum_{k\in\Lambda_N}\widehat u(k)\chi_k(x),$$
with $\widehat u(k)$ the Fourier coefficients of clause (c) of
[[def-gr-periodic-torus-and-sobolev-spaces]]; the second expression is a finite
sum, so $P_Nu\in X_N$; and $P_N:X_N\to X_N$ is the identity.
$P_N$ is called the **Galerkin (Fourier) projection**.

The definition fixes the projection only. Its self-adjointness,
derivative-commutation and operator-norm properties are proved in
[[lem-gr-galerkin-projection-properties]].

derivations.claim: (Algebraic properties (a).) Linearity is immediate since coefficients are linear in $u$. For the pairing, [L1] and the finiteness of $\Lambda_N$ give $\langle P_Nu,v\rangle_2=\sum_{k\in\Lambda_N}\widehat u(k)\cdot\overline{\widehat v(k)}$ and $\langle u,P_Nv\rangle_2=\sum_{l\in\Lambda_N}\widehat u(l)\cdot\overline{\widehat v(l)}$ after reindexing $l\mapsto-l$ and using [L3]; the two sums are equal. Since the coefficients in $\Lambda_N$ are unchanged, $P_N^2=P_N$; the kernel and range descriptions are read off from the coefficient isometry.

(Derivative commutation (b).) For $|\alpha|\le s$ and $u\in H^s$, both $D^\alpha u\in H^{s-|\alpha|}\subseteq L^2$ and $P_Nu\in X_N$ are defined; by [L2] the Fourier coefficient of $P_ND^\alpha u$ at $k$ is $(ik)^\alpha\widehat u(k)$ for $k\in\Lambda_N$ and $0$ otherwise, and that of $D^\alpha P_Nu$ is $(ik)^\alpha\widehat u(k)$ for $k\in\Lambda_N$ and $0$ otherwise, since $P_Nu$ is a finite trigonometric polynomial whose derivatives have the stated coefficients. Equality of coefficients gives (b).

(Contraction (c) and convergence (d).) For $u\in H^r$, [L2] and the definition of $P_N$ give $\|P_Nu\|_{H^r}^2=\sum_{k\in\Lambda_N}q^r_k|\widehat u(k)|^2\le\sum_kq^r_k|\widehat u(k)|^2=\|u\|_{H^r}^2$, which is (c). Similarly $\|u-P_Nu\|_{H^r}^2=\sum_{k\notin\Lambda_N}q^r_k|\widehat u(k)|^2$ is the tail of the convergent series $\sum_kq^r_k|\widehat u(k)|^2$, hence tends to $0$ as $N\to\infty$ with $\Lambda_N$ increasing to $\mathbb Z^3$; this is (d).

(Tail bound (e).) For $|k|>N$ and $|\alpha|\le s-1$, $|k^\alpha|^2\le(1+|k|^2)^{s-1}$, so $q^{s-1}_k\le(s+1)^3(1+|k|^2)^{s-1}\le(s+1)^32(1+N^2)^{-1}(1+|k|^2)^s$ because $(1+|k|^2)\ge1+N^2$; hence $\|u-P_Nu\|_{H^{s-1}}^2\le2(s+1)^3(1+N^2)^{-1}\sum_k(1+|k|^2)^s|\widehat u(k)|^2\le C_s^2(1+N^2)^{-1}\|u\|_{H^s}^2$ by the norm equivalence [L2]. Taking square roots gives (e).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let integers $s\ge m\ge0$ satisfy $s-m>3/2$, and
let $u\in H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ with the objects and notation of
[[def-gr-periodic-torus-and-sobolev-spaces]]. Then:

**(a)** There is a unique representative $u^*\in C^m(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$
of the class $u$, and for every $|\alpha|\le m$ the series
$\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(ik)^\alpha\widehat u(k)\chi_k$ converges absolutely and
uniformly on $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ to $D^\alpha u^*$; moreover there is
$C=C(s,m,N)$ with
$$\|u^*\|_{C^m}\le C\,\|u\|_{H^s}.$$

**(b)** Writing $d(x,y):=\min\{\,|x-y+2\pi l|:l\in\mathbb Z^3\,\}$ for the
induced metric on $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ and fixing
$0<\theta\le\min\{1,s-m-\tfrac32\}$, there is $C'=C'(s,m,N,\theta)$ with
$$\bigl|D^\alpha u^*(x)-D^\alpha u^*(y)\bigr|\le C'\,\|u\|_{H^s}\,d(x,y)^\theta\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb T^3_{2\pi},\ |\alpha|\le m).$$

**(c)** The assignment $u\mapsto u^*$ is linear; and if $(u_j)$ is a sequence in
$H^s$ with $u_j\to u$ in $H^s$, then $u_j^*\to u^*$ uniformly together with all
derivatives of order at most $m$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]) for the quotient, product-measure and integration
clauses below, as in [[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]].

**(a) The 2 pi-periodic torus.** Let $\mathbb T_{2\pi}:=\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z$
carry the quotient topology, and let
$$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}:=\mathbb T_{2\pi}\times\mathbb T_{2\pi}\times\mathbb T_{2\pi}$$
with the product topology; write $q:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ for the
quotient map and $[x]:=(x^1+2\pi\mathbb Z,x^2+2\pi\mathbb Z,x^3+2\pi\mathbb Z)$.
The map $[0,2\pi)^3\to\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, $x\mapsto[x]$, is a bijection. The
normalized product measure $\mu$ is $\mu_{\mathbb T}\otimes\mu_{\mathbb T}\otimes\mu_{\mathbb T}$,
where $\mu_{\mathbb T}$ is the normalized measure of
[[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]] transported by
$t\mapsto2\pi t$; it is a probability measure on the Borel sets of
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ and $\int f\,d\mu=(2\pi)^{-3}\int_{[0,2\pi)^3}f\circ q\,d\lambda_3$
for bounded measurable $f$ ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

**(b) Test functions and continuous classes.** For $N\ge1$ let
$C^\infty(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the set of compositions
$u\circ q$ of smooth maps $u:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^N$ that are $2\pi$-periodic
in each variable; these are the **smooth test functions** (real-valued when
$N=1$). For $m\ge0$ let $C^m(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the set of
$u\circ q$ with $u\in C^m(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^N)$ $2\pi$-periodic in each
variable ([[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]), with
$$\|u\|_{C^m}:=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\ \sup_{x\in\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}\bigl|(D^\alpha u)(x)\bigr| ,$$
where $D^\alpha$ is the multi-index derivative of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]] applied to any
periodic representative; the displayed expression is independent of the
representative.

**(c) The Hilbert space $L^2$.** For $N\ge1$ let
$L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the quotient of the set of measurable
$u$ with $\int|u|^2\,d\mu<\infty$ by the $\mu$-a.e. zero functions
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]),
with inner product $\langle u,v\rangle_2=\int u\cdot v\,d\mu$ and norm
$\|u\|_2=\langle u,u\rangle_2^{1/2}$; it is a real Hilbert space
([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]). For
$u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ and $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ the
**$k$-th Fourier coefficient** is the vector
$$\widehat u(k):=\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}u(x)\,e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)\in\mathbb C^N ,$$
where $e^{-ik\cdot x}:=\chi_{-k}$ with $\chi_k([x]):=\exp(i\,k\cdot x)$; here
$u$ is read through any representative. Write $\chi_k:\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\to\mathbb C$,
$k\in\mathbb Z^3$, for these **characters**; under the identification
$x=2\pi y$ they are the characters $\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot y)$ of
[[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]], so $(\chi_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}$
is an orthonormal basis of the complex space $L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb C)$.

**(d) Weak derivatives and the periodic Sobolev spaces.** For

derivations.claim: (Embedding control (a).) Since $k-(k-2)=2>3/2$, [L1] with $(s,m)=(k,k-2)$ gives a $C^{k-2}$ representative of $u$ and the bound $\sup|D^\gamma u|\le\|u\|_{C^{k-2}}\le C_k\|u\|_{H^k}$ for every $|\gamma|\le k-2$.

(Each Leibniz term is bounded by $\|u\|_{H^k}\|v\|_{H^k}$.) Fix $|\alpha|\le k$ and expand by [L3]. In a term $D^\beta u\,D^{\alpha-\beta}v$ two cases occur. First case, $|\beta|\ge k-1$: then $|\alpha-\beta|=|\alpha|-|\beta|\le1\le k-2$ because $k\ge3$, so by step 1.1 the second factor has $L^\infty$ norm at most $C_k\|v\|_{H^k}$ and the first has $L^2$ norm at most $\|u\|_{H^k}$; the product has $L^2$ norm at most $C_k\|u\|_{H^k}\|v\|_{H^k}$ by [L2]. Second case, $|\beta|\le k-2$: then $|\alpha-\beta|\le k$, so the first factor has $L^\infty$ norm at most $C_k\|u\|_{H^k}$ and the second $L^2$ norm at most $\|v\|_{H^k}$, with the same product bound. The two cases exhaust the possibilities, because $|\beta|\ge k-1$ and $|\alpha-\beta|\ge k-1$ simultaneously would give $|\alpha|\ge2k-2>k$ for $k\ge3$.

(Conclusion of (b).) Summing the at most $(k+1)^3$ terms of [L3] and using [L4], $\|D^\alpha(uv)\|_2\le(k+1)^3\max_\beta\binom{\alpha}{\beta}C_k\|u\|_{H^k}\|v\|_{H^k}$; taking the sum over $|\alpha|\le k$ and absorbing the finite combinatorial factor into a new $C_k$ gives (b). Each $D^\alpha(uv)$ is a sum of $L^2$ products, so $uv\in H^k$.

((c): smoothing by a classical factor.) For $\varphi\in C^k$ and $w\in H^k$, Leibniz [L3] gives $D^\alpha(\varphi w)=\sum_{\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}D^\beta\varphi\,D^{\alpha-\beta}w$; here $|D^\beta\varphi|\le\|\varphi\|_{C^k}$ pointwise and $\|D^{\alpha-\beta}w\|_2\le\|w\|_{H^k}$, so $\|D^\alpha(\varphi w)\|_2\le(k+1)^3\|\varphi\|_{C^k}\|w\|_{H^k}$; summing over $|\alpha|\le k$ gives (c).

$$\|u\|_{C^m}:=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\ \sup_{x\in\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}\bigl|(D^\alpha u)(x)\bigr| ,$$
where $D^\alpha$ is the multi-index derivative of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]] applied to any
periodic representative; the displayed expression is independent of the
representative.

**(c) The Hilbert space $L^2$.** For $N\ge1$ let
$L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the quotient of the set of measurable
$u$ with $\int|u|^2\,d\mu<\infty$ by the $\mu$-a.e. zero functions
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]),
with inner product $\langle u,v\rangle_2=\int u\cdot v\,d\mu$ and norm
$\|u\|_2=\langle u,u\rangle_2^{1/2}$; it is a real Hilbert space
([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]). For
$u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ and $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ the
**$k$-th Fourier coefficient** is the vector
$$\widehat u(k):=\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}u(x)\,e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)\in\mathbb C^N ,$$
where $e^{-ik\cdot x}:=\chi_{-k}$ with $\chi_k([x]):=\exp(i\,k\cdot x)$; here
$u$ is read through any representative. Write $\chi_k:\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\to\mathbb C$,
$k\in\mathbb Z^3$, for these **characters**; under the identification
$x=2\pi y$ they are the characters $\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot y)$ of
[[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]], so $(\chi_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}$
is an orthonormal basis of the complex space $L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb C)$.

**(d) Weak derivatives and the periodic Sobolev spaces.** For
$u,v\in L^1(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R)$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^3$ say that
$v$ is the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}v\,\varphi\,d\mu$$
for every $\varphi\in C^\infty(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R)$, where $D^\alpha\varphi$
is the multi-index derivative of the periodic representative
([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]] records the
Euclidean analogue). For an integer $s\ge0$ let
$$H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N):=\Bigl\{u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N):\ \text{for every }|\alpha|\le s\text{ there is }v_\alpha\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)\text{ with }v_\alpha=D^\alpha u\Bigr\},$$
the vector-valued weak derivative being componentwise, and put
$$\|u\|_{H^s}:=\Bigl(\sum_{|\alpha|\le s}\|D^\alpha u\|_2^2\Bigr)^{1/2}.$$
The classes $L^2\subseteq L^1$ on the probability space, so the integrals in the
test identity are finite: $|\int u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu|\le\|u\|_2\|D^\alpha\varphi\|_2$
by Cauchy--Schwarz. The definition asserts neither that the weak derivative
exists nor that the two norms compared in the next item are equivalent; those
are proved in [[lem-gr-periodic-fourier-differentiation-and-norm-equivalence]].

**(e) Conventions.** $O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ open, $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ an
interval and maps $F:I\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\times O\to\mathbb R^{m'}$ are
called smooth when their representatives $F(t,q(x),u)=G(t,x,u)$ have
$G\in C^\infty$. Throughout this page the torus is always this
$2\pi$-periodic one; a statement "for every $x$" means for every point of
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, and "a.e." means $\mu$-a.e.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]) for the quotient, product-measure and integration
clauses below, as in [[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]].

**(a) The 2 pi-periodic torus.** Let $\mathbb T_{2\pi}:=\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z$
carry the quotient topology, and let
$$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}:=\mathbb T_{2\pi}\times\mathbb T_{2\pi}\times\mathbb T_{2\pi}$$
with the product topology; write $q:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ for the
quotient map and $[x]:=(x^1+2\pi\mathbb Z,x^2+2\pi\mathbb Z,x^3+2\pi\mathbb Z)$.
The map $[0,2\pi)^3\to\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, $x\mapsto[x]$, is a bijection. The
normalized product measure $\mu$ is $\mu_{\mathbb T}\otimes\mu_{\mathbb T}\otimes\mu_{\mathbb T}$,
where $\mu_{\mathbb T}$ is the normalized measure of
[[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]] transported by
$t\mapsto2\pi t$; it is a probability measure on the Borel sets of
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ and $\int f\,d\mu=(2\pi)^{-3}\int_{[0,2\pi)^3}f\circ q\,d\lambda_3$
for bounded measurable $f$ ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

in each variable; these are the **smooth test functions** (real-valued when
$N=1$). For $m\ge0$ let $C^m(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the set of

variable ([[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]), with
$$\|u\|_{C^m}:=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\ \sup_{x\in\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}\bigl|(D^\alpha u)(x)\bigr| ,$$
where $D^\alpha$ is the multi-index derivative of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]] applied to any
periodic representative; the displayed expression is independent of the
representative.

**(c) The Hilbert space $L^2$.** For $N\ge1$ let
$L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the quotient of the set of measurable

([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]),
with inner product $\langle u,v\rangle_2=\int u\cdot v\,d\mu$ and norm
$\|u\|_2=\langle u,u\rangle_2^{1/2}$; it is a real Hilbert space
([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]). For
$u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ and $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ the
**$k$-th Fourier coefficient** is the vector
$$\widehat u(k):=\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}u(x)\,e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)\in\mathbb C^N ,$$
where $e^{-ik\cdot x}:=\chi_{-k}$ with $\chi_k([x]):=\exp(i\,k\cdot x)$; here
$u$ is read through any representative. Write $\chi_k:\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\to\mathbb C$,
$k\in\mathbb Z^3$, for these **characters**; under the identification
$x=2\pi y$ they are the characters $\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot y)$ of
[[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]], so $(\chi_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}$
is an orthonormal basis of the complex space $L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb C)$.

**(d) Weak derivatives and the periodic Sobolev spaces.** For
$u,v\in L^1(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R)$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^3$ say that
$v$ is the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}v\,\varphi\,d\mu$$
for every $\varphi\in C^\infty(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R)$, where $D^\alpha\varphi$
is the multi-index derivative of the periodic representative
([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]] records the
Euclidean analogue). For an integer $s\ge0$ let
$$H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N):=\Bigl\{u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N):\ \text{for every }|\alpha|\le s\text{ there is }v_\alpha\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)\text{ with }v_\alpha=D^\alpha u\Bigr\},$$
the vector-valued weak derivative being componentwise, and put
$$\|u\|_{H^s}:=\Bigl(\sum_{|\alpha|\le s}\|D^\alpha u\|_2^2\Bigr)^{1/2}.$$

by Cauchy--Schwarz. The definition asserts neither that the weak derivative
exists nor that the two norms compared in the next item are equivalent; those
are proved in [[lem-gr-periodic-fourier-differentiation-and-norm-equivalence]].

**(e) Conventions.** $O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ open, $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ an
interval and maps $F:I\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\times O\to\mathbb R^{m'}$ are
called smooth when their representatives $F(t,q(x),u)=G(t,x,u)$ have
$G\in C^\infty$. Throughout this page the torus is always this
$2\pi$-periodic one; a statement "for every $x$" means for every point of

derivations.claim: (Composition bound (a).) Fix $|\alpha|\le r\le s$ and expand $D^\alpha(F(t,\cdot,u))$ by [L3]. In each term of the expansion, by [L4] at most one factor has order $\ge r-1$; every factor of order $\le s-2$ has $L^\infty$ norm at most $C_sR$ by [L1] and the exceptional factor, of order at most $r\le s$, has $L^2$ norm at most $\|u\|_{H^s}$ by [L1]; coefficients are bounded by $M$. Hence each term has $L^2$ norm at most $M C_s^{r}(1+R)^{r}\|u\|_{H^s}^{\varepsilon}$ with $\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}$, which is at most $C_{s,R}(1+\|u\|_{H^s})$; the finitely many terms of the expansion for all $|\alpha|\le r$ give (a) after enlarging the constant.

(Difference bound (b).) For $u(t),v(t)$ with values in the convex compact $C_1$ put $u_\vartheta:=v(t)+\vartheta(u(t)-v(t))$ for $\vartheta\in[0,1]$; its values lie in $C_1\subseteq O$ and $\|u_\vartheta\|_{H^s}\le(1-\vartheta)\|v(t)\|_{H^s}+\vartheta\|u(t)\|_{H^s}\le R$. The mean-value formula $F(u)-F(v)=\int_0^1DF(t,\cdot,u_\vartheta)(u-v)\,d\vartheta$ holds pointwise and hence in $L^2$; by step 1.1 applied to the smooth coefficient $DF$, $\|DF(t,\cdot,u_\vartheta)\|_{H^{k}}\le C_R$, and by [L2] applied with the finite-measure $L^2$ bound, $\|DF(u_\vartheta)(u-v)\|_{H^{k}}\le C_R\|u-v\|_{H^{k}}$; integrating in $\vartheta$ gives (b).

(Commutator bound (c).) By the Leibniz-rule part of [L3], $[D^\alpha,A(u)]w=\sum_{0<\gamma\le\alpha}c_\gamma\,D^\gamma(A(t,\cdot,u))\,D^{\alpha-\gamma}w$. For each $\gamma\ne0$: the expansion of $D^\gamma(A(u))$ has terms with total order $|\gamma|\le k\le s$, so by [L4] each term has at most one factor of order $\ge s-1$ and the remaining factors have $L^\infty$ bounds $C_sR$; hence $\|D^\gamma(A(u))\|_2\le C_R$. Two cases exhaust the possibilities: if $|\gamma|\le s-2$, then $\sup|D^\gamma(A(t,\cdot,u))|\le C_R$ by [L1] (applied to the composition, whose $H^s$ norm is bounded by step 1.1 with $r=s$), while $\|D^{\alpha-\gamma}w\|_2\le\|w\|_{H^{|\alpha|-1}}$ because $|\alpha-\gamma|\le|\alpha|-1$; if $|\gamma|\ge s-1$, then $|\gamma|\le k=s-1$ forces $|\gamma|=s-1$ and $|\alpha-\gamma|\le k-(s-1)=0$, so $\|D^\gamma(A(u))\|_2\le C_R$ as just computed and $\|w\|_\infty\le C\|w\|_{H^{k}}$ with $k=s-1=j$ in the notation of the previous paragraph, hence at most $C\|w\|_{H^{|\alpha|-1}}$ because $|\alpha|=s-1$ in this case. Summing the finitely many terms gives (c).

(Coefficient product (d).) Fix $|\gamma|\le j\le k$ and expand $D^\gamma(A(u)w)=\sum_{\delta\le\gamma}\binom{\gamma}{\delta}D^\delta(A(u))\,D^{\gamma-\delta}w$ by [L3]. If $|\delta|\ge s-1$, then $|\delta|=s-1=k=j$ and $\delta=\gamma$, $|\gamma-\delta|=0$, so $\|D^\delta(A(u))\|_2\le C_R$ by step 1.1 with $r=k$ and $\|w\|_\infty\le\|w\|_{H^{j}}$ by [L1] with $(s,m)=(j,0)$; if $|\delta|\le s-2$ then $\sup|D^\delta(A(u))|\le C_R$ by [L1] applied to the $H^s$ class $A(u)$ (whose $H^s$ norm is bounded by step 1.1 with $r=s$) and $\|D^{\gamma-\delta}w\|_2\le\|w\|_{H^j}$. Summing the finitely many terms gives (d).
